Pour laundry detergent to the fill line your label gives for your load size, not to the brim of the cap, and the same jug lasts for more loads. In the bathroom, use a small dab of shampoo, a pea-size bit of toothpaste, and a foaming pump filled with soap thinned with water.

Every extra splash of detergent or squeeze of shampoo is product you paid for and then rinsed down the drain.

The dose on a detergent label is set for typical wash conditions and gives the best cleaning, says the American Cleaning Institute, the trade group for cleaning-product makers. Pour past it for an ordinary load and the jug just empties sooner. Too much detergent can even leave residue on your clothes, Whirlpool says.

Say your jug’s label promises 64 loads at the medium-load line, and you’ve been pouring 50% more than that each time. The jug runs out after about 43 loads. Pour to the line and you get all 64 loads instead of 43, about 50% more, so two jugs now do the work of three.

Start with the fill line for your load size, using a high-efficiency (HE) detergent if your washer is an HE model. Then use less for a small or lightly soiled load or soft water, and more for a large or heavily soiled load or hard water (water high in minerals), as the institute advises.

Before your next load, find the fill line your detergent’s label gives for the load you wash most, and pour to it every time.

#8458. Buy a Rental for Its Cash Flow – Treat Price Gains as a Bonus

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A rental that loses money each month is a bet that home prices will rise, and when they stall or fall, you keep covering the shortfall or sell at a loss. Buy one whose rent covers every cost, from the mortgage to repairs and vacancies, and treat any rise in value as extra.

Picture an investor who bought a condo in 2006 expecting price gains of 10% a year to make up for rent that fell $1,000 a month short of its costs. By 2011 the condo was worth 30% less, and the investor sold at a loss after paying $60,000 to cover five years of shortfalls.

A rental with negative cash flow, meaning rent that falls short of its costs, pays off only if prices climb fast enough to cover the shortfall. Every repair and every vacancy adds to the shortfall, and borrowing makes a price drop worse. With 20% down, a 20% fall in price wipes out your whole down payment, because the loan doesn’t shrink when the price does.

The Federal Housing Finance Agency’s national index of home prices fell nearly 20% from its April 2007 peak by March 2011. In Austin, Texas, home prices jumped nearly 60% from 2020 to 2022, then the median price fell 22% from its pandemic peak by mid-2025, the Texas Real Estate Research Center found. Over the long run, most of what houses earned came from rent. In a typical year from 1890 to 2006, a house returned about 9% after inflation, with 7.7% from rent, before expenses, and only 1.3% from rising prices, a Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia working paper found.

So buy only a property whose rent covers the mortgage, taxes, insurance, and a budget for repairs and vacancies. In an expensive market, that may mean buying in a city where rent still covers a mortgage. Run the full numbers before you make an offer. If the rent falls short, put more down to shrink the payment, or wait for a property that pays its own way.

Count the loan balance you pay down each month, and any rise in value, as your long-run gain, not as money toward the monthly costs.

You can hold a rental that covers its own costs through a slump, because the rent, not your paycheck, keeps paying the loan.

#8457. Skip Fabric Softener & Dryer Sheets – Most Loads Don’t Need Them

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Stop buying fabric softener and dryer sheets by habit. Softener can make towels less absorbent and leave a residue that traps odor in workout clothes, and most other laundry comes out fine without either. For static, dry your synthetic fabrics in their own load and take them out as soon as they’re dry.

A $13 jug of Downy covers 190 medium loads, and a $10 box of Bounce holds 240 sheets. A family that washes the roughly 300 loads a year ENERGY STAR says is average, using a medium dose and one sheet each time, spends about 11 cents a load, or about $33 a year.

Both work by coating fibers so they feel smoother and cling less, and that coating is the catch. Consumer Reports says liquid softener leaves a film that makes towels less absorbent and more flammable. Nike says softener leaves a residue on workout clothes that traps odor-causing bacteria and that sheets clog the fabric, so detergent has a harder time getting in. CHOICE, Australia’s consumer group, warns that softeners can also weaken the flame resistance of children’s sleepwear.

So check the care label before reaching for softener, and keep it away from towels, workout clothes, kids’ pajamas, and anything labeled flame resistant. Softener changes how fabric feels, not how clean it gets, so the rest of the wash can skip it too.

For static, the fix costs nothing. Whirlpool, the appliance maker, says synthetics such as polyester and nylon are especially prone to static and that over-drying makes it worse. So dry them in a load of their own on low heat or the dryer’s moisture-sensing setting.

Wool dryer balls, sold as a reusable swap for sheets, start at about $9 for a set of six, roughly a quarter of the $33 a year that softener and sheets cost. Whirlpool says wool balls help prevent static by absorbing moisture. But a 2016 test by Consumer NZ found no less static and no softer clothes with dryer balls. CHOICE’s 2024 test found that none of the balls it tried did much for drying time or energy use. Treat them as optional.

Use up the jug and box you have, then leave both off the shopping list and keep about $33 a year.

#8456. Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

During the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They launched the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8455. Screen Tenants by a Standard You Wrote Before Listing – Not by First Impressions

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Before you list a rental, write down the income, credit, landlord references, and eviction history an applicant needs. Then verify each one for every applicant instead of taking the application’s word for it. One written standard helps you pick tenants who pay and keeps your decisions within fair housing law.

Turning away the wrong applicant costs a little more time with the unit empty. Removing the wrong tenant can take a court case and months of lost rent.

A standard set before you meet anyone keeps a good first impression from outweighing a bad rental history. Say an applicant charms you at the showing, but their last landlord reports two months of unpaid rent. A standard that asks for on-time rent at the last two rentals rules them out, and the unit goes to the next complete application.

The Fair Housing Act bars most landlords from turning anyone away because of race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, or having children under 18. A standard applied the same way to everyone is your record of why you turned someone down. In many states and cities, source-of-income laws also bar refusing an applicant whose housing voucher pays part of the rent.

If you check criminal records, write down which convictions count and how far back you’ll look, within your state’s and city’s rules. New Jersey and New York City make most landlords wait to run a criminal check until they’ve offered the unit, pending its result, to an applicant who meets the rest of the standard.

Use one written application for everyone, and keep its fee within what your state allows.

Hand every applicant the standard in writing before you take a fee or run a check. Washington requires landlords to share their criteria, in writing or posted, before any screening, and elsewhere it spares an applicant who can’t qualify a wasted fee.

#8454. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 27

Most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents from the last seven days.

A tiger killed two farmers in separate incidents about five kilometers apart within 24 hours in the eastern corner of India’s Maharashtra state.

Sixty-year-old farmer Nana Kambadi was killed by a tiger while working in his field on Saturday evening. The following evening, Premila Mahadole, 40, was attacked while harvesting rice. Her body was later found in the field. Officials suspect it was the same tiger, but this has not been confirmed.

The back-to-back killings have thrown residents across the district into a panic, according to the Times of India. At this time of year, many are out in their fields harvesting rice at the edges of forests.

The death toll from human-animal conflicts in just this part of Maharashtra state has now risen to 35 in 2026, according to officials.

A family herd of wild Indian elephants. Photo: Shutterstock

An elephant killed a man who was trying to drive a herd of 23 elephants away from his village in Jharkhand state in eastern India. According to forest officials, the elephant seized Nicholas Topno, 40, with its trunk, dragged him nearly 500m, and trampled him. The herd, which included five calves, had been damaging crops in the area. Officials had been monitoring the movements for several days and warned residents not to approach. Our team has been monitoring its movement round the clock for the last five days, but some villagers still ventured close to the elephants,” forest officer Shekhar Singh told the Times of India. Because bear attacks continue to be a problem in many parts of Japan, officials have warned residents to avoid unnecessary outings. #8452. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

#8451. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder.  And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me)

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

Interesting. I know very little about this topic, but as I read my thoughts immediately went to the evolutionary biologist Robert Sapolsky and his book The Trouble With Testosterone. I would encourage you to go down that pathway and add it into your thinking. I’m curious what the Bolt people would say to these arguments.

It has been some time since I read the book so I got some LLM summaries to refresh me on why many evolutionary biologist consider testosterone an expensive biological tax. I’m going to paste some of it here:

In the wild, maintaining high testosterone levels is akin to driving a car with the engine red-lining. It provides short-term power for mating and fighting, but it wears down the machinery (the body) much faster. Here is a breakdown of the specific evolutionary costs Sapolsky and other biologists highlight, focusing on the immune system and metabolic “taxes.” 1. The Immunocompetence Handicap This is the central theory explaining why high testosterone is costly. The “Handicap Principle” suggests that because testosterone suppresses the immune system, only males with superior genetics can afford to maintain high levels of it. The Trade-off: Energy is finite. The body must choose between investing in survival (immunity, cell repair) or reproduction (muscle mass, aggression, mating displays). Testosterone forces the body to prioritize reproduction at the expense of survival. The “Honest Signal”: High T features (like a peacock’s tail or a stag’s massive muscles) are “honest signals” to females because they are dangerous to possess. The male is essentially saying, “Look at how strong my genes are—I can handicap my own immune system with this much testosterone and still be standing.” Parasitic Load: In wild primate studies, males with the highest testosterone often have the highest burden of intestinal parasites. Their immune systems are less efficient at fighting off low-level infections because their energy is diverted elsewhere. 2. Metabolic & Physiological Costs Beyond just the immune system, high testosterone extracts a heavy toll on the body’s daily maintenance. Metabolic Burn: Testosterone is metabolically expensive. It forces the body to build and maintain lean muscle mass which burns calories at a much higher rate than fat. In a food-scarce environment (which is most of evolutionary history), having high T is a risk; you are more likely to starve during a famine. The “Good Cholesterol” Crash: Testosterone generally lowers HDL (good cholesterol). Sapolsky notes that this is one reason why males across many species die younger than females. The hormone that helps you win the fight today clogs your arteries for tomorrow. 3. Behavioral “Taxes” High testosterone lowers the threshold for risk-taking, which carries a direct survival cost. Injury and Mortality: High-T males are more conspicuous and more likely to engage in risky confrontations. In the wild, “winning” a fight often leaves a victor injured, making them susceptible to infection (which their T-suppressed immune system is now less equipped to fight). Parental Investment: Evolutionarily, there is often an inverse relationship between testosterone and parental care. High T drives mating effort (seeking new partners) rather than parenting effort (caring for offspring). In species where offspring need high investment, high T can actually be an evolutionary disadvantage if the offspring die from neglect. Summary of the Trap The “trouble” Sapolsky identifies is that while high testosterone might help a male pass on genes (by winning a mate), it actively works against his staying alive. The Irony: Pro-TRT (Testosterone Replacement Therapy) arguments often frame high T as the key to “health” and “vitality.” From an evolutionary standpoint, nature views high T as the exact opposite: a calculated health risk taken solely to reproduce before you die.

I hope this is good food for thought and discussion. Thanks for your years of great blogging MMM!

#8450. Marriage, a Baby, or a Second Income? Change Your W-4 Within Weeks

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Payroll withholds tax for the household your W-4 describes until you hand in a new one. Within weeks of a wedding, a divorce, a new baby, a second job, or new side income, run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator. Give your employer the new W-4 it fills in while enough paychecks remain to spread the correction.

Every paycheck after the change is withheld at the old setting. The gap grows each payday, and the paydays left to close it shrink.

Each employer withholds based only on its own paycheck and what your W-4 tells it, such as your filing status and children. So a spouse’s pay, a second job, or side income on your return calls for more withholding. A divorce final by December 31 usually does too, since you’ll be taxed as unmarried for the whole year while payroll still withholds as married. A new child, or a spouse with no income, lets you have less withheld.

Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with your latest pay stub. It counts the new deductions for tips, overtime, seniors, and car loan interest, then fills in a new W-4 that payroll has about a month to start using. When a change like a divorce or a second job leaves you short for the year, the IRS requires the new form within 10 days.

Say newlyweds earn $60,000 each, are paid every two weeks, have no other income, and take the standard deduction. Both switch to married filing jointly in January and skip Step 2, the two-jobs step. Each employer gives its paycheck the couple’s whole standard deduction and lowest brackets, so by our math they end the year about $4,400 short. Fix it in July, and each spouse’s 13 remaining paychecks need about $170 more withheld apiece. Wait until October, and each spouse’s last six need about $360 apiece.

Side income from freelance or gig work has nothing withheld. Extra withholding in Step 4(c) can cover its tax, and when that’s more than your paychecks can spare, pay the rest in quarterly estimated payments. The IRS’s penalty rules count withholding as paid evenly through the year, so raising it in the fall also covers spring’s due dates, which a late estimated payment can’t.

Then rerun the estimator in late December, as the IRS advises, so a catch-up amount sized for a few paychecks doesn’t over-withhold all of next year.

#8449. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#8447. Skin Care Works by Its Ingredients, Not Its Price – Buy Them at the Drugstore

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Skin care results come from a short list of proven ingredients, like retinoids, vitamin C, and sunscreen, not from the price. Drugstore brands sell them, often for a fraction of luxury prices. Before you buy, check the label for the active ingredient and its strength, then pick the cheapest product that lists both.

A luxury retinol night cream that lists 0.3% retinol costs $160 an ounce. Drugstore night serums with the same 0.3% retinol cost $30 to $40 an ounce.

Choosing a drugstore serum over the cream saves $120 to $130 an ounce, and the cream’s higher price doesn’t guarantee better results. The American Academy of Dermatology says products that work come at every price, and its dermatologists rank sunscreen and moisturizer as the two most effective anti-aging buys.

Beyond those two, choose products by their active ingredient. In a 2025 study in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, dermatologists narrowed 318 skin care ingredients to 23 they agree on for problems like wrinkles, acne, and dark spots.

Three of the 23 are drugstore staples. Match the one on the label to what you want to fix:

Over-the-counter retinol products don’t have to state their strength on the label, so choose one that does and start with the lowest strength you can find. For any of the three, compare products by the ingredient and its strength, not the jar or the scent, and buy the cheapest one that matches. Makeup is a separate question, since how it looks on you is part of what you pay for.

Keep the daily routine to a cleanser, a moisturizer, and a sunscreen labeled broad-spectrum with SPF 30 or higher. A moisturizer with the same label counts as both. After a few weeks, add one active ingredient for the concern that bothers you most, since starting several at once can irritate your skin. Deep, painful acne or acne that scars needs a dermatologist from the start, because store-bought products are unlikely to clear it.

Give each new active ingredient at least six weeks, and if three months pass with no change, see a board-certified dermatologist instead of buying a pricier product.

#8446. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8445. Buying a Rental in Another State – Hire Your Local Team Before You Offer

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Buying a rental in a cheaper state can turn a modest budget into a house whose rent covers its costs, but you can’t drive by to check on it. Pick the market by its numbers, hire a local agent, inspector, and property manager before you offer, and see the house on live video or in person before closing.

What you’d learn on a visit, from the roof’s condition to the for-rent signs on the block, has to come from numbers you can check and people you hire.

Look for a city that’s adding jobs and residents. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Economy at a Glance tables track its metro area’s jobs, and Census QuickFacts tracks its population. Compare a year’s rent with the price, the test that picks out cities where rent still covers the mortgage. Read the state’s landlord-tenant law on deposits and evictions.

Then hire your local team before you make an offer, the property manager first, since a good one knows which blocks keep tenants. Say an investor in San Jose likes a $190,000 house in Indianapolis that would rent for $1,650 a month. The manager she hires first warns her that houses on that block sit empty for months between tenants and steers her to a house two streets over.

Interview managers the way you’d interview a job candidate. Call owners whose rentals they manage, and check any license the state requires. Add an agent who works with investors and knows what nearby houses rent for, an independent inspector you hire yourself, and a mortgage lender that will finance a rental in that state. A turnkey rental, one a company has already renovated and rented, calls for checks of its own.

For each house, find out the property tax a rental would owe and get a landlord insurance quote. The Government Accountability Office found that average homeowners insurance premiums in southern coastal areas rose at least 25% from 2019 to 2024, against 3% nationwide.

Have your agent walk you through the house on a live video call before you offer. Write the offer with an inspection contingency, which lets you renegotiate or back out if the inspection turns up problems.

Set aside cash for whatever the inspector flagged and the rest of the first year’s repairs, and visit before closing or soon after to meet your manager and see the house.

#8444. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8443. Women’s Toiletries Often Cost More Than Men’s – Compare the Unit Prices

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

The pink tax is the extra charged for a product marketed to women when it differs from the men’s version only in color, scent, or packaging. Compare the price per ounce or per item of both versions, check that the ingredients match, and buy the cheaper one, whichever aisle you find it in.

When New York City’s Department of Consumer Affairs compared nearly 800 products sold in men’s and women’s versions in 2015, the women’s versions cost 7% more on average and 13% more for personal care. The widest gap was hair care, where women paid 48% more than men for shampoo and conditioner.

In a 2018 study of 10 personal care categories, the Government Accountability Office found women’s versions cost more in five, deodorant among them, but men’s cost more for shaving gel and nondisposable razors.

Some of the difference in the city’s study came from package size. It found men’s deodorant often sold in 2.7-ounce sticks and women’s in 2.6-ounce sticks at the same price, so compare the unit price, the cost per ounce or per item.

Say a pink four-pack of disposable razors costs $6 and the same razor in a blue six-pack costs $7.50. That’s $1.50 a razor against $1.25, so the blue pack is the cheaper buy. Then make sure the formulas match. For an antiperspirant, compare the active ingredient and strength on the Drug Facts label. For a shampoo, compare the first several ingredients, which are listed in order of amount.

In California and New York, a business can’t charge different prices for substantially similar products or services based on gender. A haircut or a dry-cleaning job can still cost more when it takes more time or skill. California’s Gender Tax Repeal Act also makes barbers, salons, tailors, and dry cleaners post prices for their standard services, and New York entitles you to a written price list on request from any service business.

Report a product priced by gender to California’s attorney general. In New York, file a complaint with the Division of Consumer Protection to seek back the difference you paid, or call its helpline at 1-800-697-1220.

Start with deodorant, the category both studies found pricier for women than for men, and compare the price per ounce of a men’s or unisex stick with the same active ingredient and strength.

#8442. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8441. Measure Your Pet’s Food – Extra Scoops Mean Bigger Food & Vet Bills

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Measure your pet’s meals with a kitchen scale or a level measuring cup, and feed the label’s amount for the weight your pet should be, not its current weight. Count treats as part of the day’s food. Eyeballed portions tend to run big, so the bag empties sooner and the extra pounds raise vet bills.

Those extra pounds are common. In the Association for Pet Obesity Prevention’s 2022 survey, veterinary professionals found 59% of dogs and 61% of cats overweight or obese.

Even a cup or scoop leaves room for error. When University of Guelph researchers had 100 dog owners measure set amounts of kibble, their portions ran from 48% too little to 152% too much, and the smallest amount, a quarter cup, gave them the most trouble.

Say the feeding chart calls for a third of a cup a day and your cat gets half a cup. That’s 50% more than the chart’s amount, so a bag meant to last two months is gone in about six weeks and your cost per day rises by the same 50%. The American Animal Hospital Association’s nutrition guidelines link obesity to arthritis and diabetes. In Banfield Pet Hospital’s 2017 report, owners of overweight dogs spent 17% more on health care and 25% more on medications than owners of healthy-weight dogs.

Weigh meals on a kitchen scale, which the same guidelines rate as more accurate than measuring cups. Weigh one level cup of the food once, and a third-cup meal is a third of that weight. With a cup, pick one the size of the portion and level it off.

Use the chart’s amount for your pet’s ideal weight, which your vet can tell you, and treat it as a starting point. The guidelines base a pet’s calories on its ideal weight and warn that the amounts on labels can run high.

Keep treats to 10% of the day’s calories, the guidelines’ limit, or use pieces of the day’s measured kibble as treats. A bowl that stays full all day can’t be measured, so switch to set meals.

Then check your pet’s shape. You should be able to feel its ribs but not see them, and see a waist behind them from above. If you have to press to find the ribs, feed a little less, whatever the chart says.

#8440. Gifted Stock Carries Your Cost Basis – Give It to Someone in the 0% Bracket

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

To give stock, transfer the shares to the recipient’s brokerage account or a child’s custodial account. Your cost basis, what you paid, goes with them, so the recipient owes tax on your gain when they sell. Give appreciated shares to someone whose low income means 0% tax on long-term gains, and sell losing shares yourself to deduct the loss.

The gain you built is then taxed at the recipient’s rate, not yours, so the right recipient can owe nothing.

Say shares you bought years ago for $2,000 are worth $10,000 now, and you pay 15% on long-term gains, those on investments held over a year. Selling them yourself costs $1,200 in federal tax on the $8,000 gain.

Give them to your daughter in her first full year of work after college. The time you’ve held them counts as hers, so she gets long-term rates at once. If her taxable income, the gain included, stays low enough for the 0% long-term rate, she owes no federal tax on it. The kiddie tax limits this for anyone under 18, and for 18-year-olds and full-time students under 24 whose earnings cover no more than half their support. It taxes their investment income above a small yearly amount at a parent’s rate when that’s higher.

To make the gift, you’ll need the recipient’s brokerage name and account number for your broker’s online gift tool or form. For a child, open a custodial account, often called a UTMA or UGMA account, in their name. The shares become the child’s the day you give them, and the custodian manages them until the child comes of age.

Giving over $19,000 in a year to one person other than your spouse means filing a gift tax return, but you owe tax only once your lifetime gifts pass a multimillion-dollar exemption. Shares given to a charity or a donor-advised fund leave no one owing tax on the gain, since charities pay no income tax. Heirs who inherit shares in a taxable account get the shares’ value at death as their basis, so the gain before then goes untaxed.

Never give shares worth less than you paid. Neither of you can deduct the drop that came before the gift. Sell them, deduct the loss on your own return, and give the cash.

Before the transfer, open your broker’s cost basis page and send only the batches of shares that have gained.

#8439. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.
