I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

The “Never 100” rule and “Straight A” strategy have become cornerstones of my financial habits, helping me live below my means and automate my savings and giving. It was perfect for someone like myself who didn’t want a complicated, jargon-filled financial class – and wasn’t going to sign up for an intense ‘shame & blame’ session either.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

Dylan is a devoted husband, father, and Christian leader who serves in lay-ministry at Calvary Chapel of Westmoreland County. With a background in marketing for influential organizations such as The Navigators ministry and Highmark Health, he brings a unique perspective to his passion for developing practical discipleship tools. He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.

#8437. Line-Dry Your Laundry – The Average Electric Dryer Costs About $125 a Year

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Hang most of your laundry on a folding rack or a line, since an electric dryer costs about 40 cents a load at average U.S. electricity prices. A $30 rack pays for itself after about 75 loads you hang instead, and you can still keep the dryer for towels, sheets, and rainy weeks.

The average electric dryer uses just over 690 kilowatt-hours of electricity a year, a field study the Northwest Energy Efficiency Alliance published in 2026 found. At the average U.S. residential rate of 18.16 cents per kilowatt-hour in August 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, that comes to about $125 a year.

The same study found the average household runs 307 full drying cycles a year, so each load costs about 40 cents to dry, and a load you hang costs nothing. A gas dryer costs less to run than an electric one, so hanging its loads saves less.

At 40 cents a load, a couple who wash seven loads a week and hang five of them save $2 a week, or $104 a year, and cut their drying bill by more than 70%. Their $30 folding rack pays for itself in 15 weeks.

You don’t need a yard. A folding rack stands in a corner, a wall-mounted rack folds flat when it’s empty, and shirts dry on hangers hooked over the shower rod. A retractable line can stretch across a tub or a balcony, but check your lease or homeowners association’s rules for a ban on outdoor clotheslines before you hang one outside.

If you hang towels too, take them down while they’re still a little damp, then soften them with 10 minutes in the dryer. Air-drying also spares your clothes the dryer’s heat, which helps them last longer.

For the loads you still dry, clean the lint screen every time and use the moisture-sensor or auto-dry setting instead of a timer, so the dryer stops once the clothes are dry. Run those loads back to back, too, while the drum still holds the last load’s heat.

Hang workout clothes and other lightweight synthetics first, since they dry faster than towels or jeans. At 40 cents a load, every weekly load you hang instead of drying saves about $21 a year.

#8436. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.

#8434. Spanish Team Bags First Ascent of Jugal II

Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain have completed the first ascent of 6,518m Jugal II.

According to Spanish media, the team climbed via the east-southeast side and reached the summit on October 26. One day later, they returned to base camp, their home team told Diario de Navarra. Zabalza and Urabain had explored the area in the spring of 2024, but bad weather prevented them from attempting the peak. The team will share more details when they’re back home.

Jugal II was also the planned goal for Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet, who left for the area three weeks ago. Originally, the team wanted to climb Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region. Recent storms and floods had cut trails and swept away bridges in that area, so they had to seek an alternative.

ExplorersWeb caught up with Meroi as she and Benet reached a lodge to seek shelter from the heavy rain.

“We’re on our way to Kathmandu, and we are with the Spaniards,” she confirmed. As Nives explained, they all attempted the climb, and the Spanish team reached the summit, while the Italians retreated on the previous day. Until now, there has been no news from the Italians since Tine Cuder of Slovenia, the third team member, fell ill and left the expedition two weeks ago.

Left to right, Nives Meroi, Tine Cuder, and Romano Benet in Kathmandu. Photo: Romano Benet

The Jugal Himal is just northeast of Kathmandu, on the Tibetan border. Surprisingly accessible for a previously unclimbed peak, it’s reachable by bus and a few days’ trekking. Jugal I and II opened to foreign expeditions in 2023. In spring 2024, veteran South Korean climber Um Hong-gil led a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi to both unclimbed Jugals. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II. According to The Himalayan Database, Jugal II remained unclimbed.

The main peaks in Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

#8433. Wash Full Loads on Cold – Heating Water Is About 90% of a Washer’s Energy

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Heating the water takes most of the energy your washing machine uses, so set everyday loads to cold and run the washer only when it’s full. Save hot water for the few loads that need it to kill germs or cut grease.

The washer’s motor is the cheap part of a load. Energy Star puts water heating at about 90% of a clothes washer’s energy use.

Take a standard washer, which uses about 20 gallons a load by Energy Star’s count, and assume a hot wash heats half of that, 10 gallons, from 50 to 120 degrees. With an electric water heater, that takes about 1.7 kilowatt-hours, roughly 30 cents at 17.23 cents per kilowatt-hour, the 2025 average residential price from the Energy Information Administration.

A gas water heater that gets about 80% of its fuel’s heat into the water does the same job for about 11 cents, at the agency’s 2025 residential average of $15.34 per thousand cubic feet. Switching from hot to warm can cut either cost in half, Energy Star says, and the cold cycle cuts the cost further. An Energy Star front-loader uses about half the water of a top-loader with an agitator, so switching it to cold saves less.

Hot water is still worth paying for on a few loads. During a stomach bug, the CDC says to wash clothes, towels, or bedding with vomit or stool on them in hot water on the longest cycle, then machine dry them on the highest heat. Greasy work clothes are the other case, since Energy Star’s advice to wash cold makes an exception for oily stains. Wash everything else on cold, with a detergent made for cold water, as the South Carolina Energy Office advises.

Run fewer, fuller loads, too, and start them at night or on weekends if your utility charges less at those times. A washer uses about the same energy whatever the size of the load, Energy Star says, so two half loads cost about twice what one full load does. If a small load can’t wait, set the water level to match it. For the rest of the electric bill, start with heating, cooling, and hot water.

A family that switches eight warm loads a week to cold saves up to $61 a year with an electric water heater, or $22 with gas.

#8431. The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Social Security

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who currently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

First let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:

At that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re new to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:

Whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result!  Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a big lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

The net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a big boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all issues. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that new users will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions

If you log in to check on your Social Security account when you’re still young, you’ll see some confusing stuff – basically it tells you how much your payout will be if you continue working and contributing for a ridiculously long 35 year period!Your benefit is calculated by taking an average of your 35 highest years of earnings, which sounds bleak for people like me who only worked a ten-year career, because in theory that average might contain mostly zeroes. But never fear because:

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35.  Look at the difference in their benefits:

So the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Something that really helped me with the mental math of Social Security is the concept of bend points.

Bend points are lifetime earnings milestones that govern how much Social Security pays out to you. For all income up to the first bend point, you get about 90 cents back from Social Security for every dollar you pay in. After that, it drops off steeply. For income between the first and second bend points, you get more like 32 cents on the dollar, and after the second bend point, you get about 15 cents.

Right now in 2026, you hit the first bend point at something like $540,000 of total lifetime earnings, and the second bend point is around $3.25 million.

The great news for early retirees is that, because Social Security’s payout formula tails off so quickly for higher earners (as you mentioned in the article), it really doesn’t matter very much that we won’t have 35 full years of contributions. Just by working a few years, we get most of the benefits. After that, it’s a game of diminishing returns where you have to work for years and years just to increase your benefit by a small amount. No thanks – I’d rather be retired!

Great question.. in the equations I showed in this article, they don’t show that more complex calculation: they are only showing how to calculate the present value of a stream of payments as it would apply *right now*.

So you’d solve the simpler equation first to get the NPV for that stream of payments on whatever day it starts, and then re-apply the NPV formula for a fixed chunk of future money, brought forward to today.

Social security Whoa Nellie! Yes, of course you can start taking SS at age 62. As mentioned above, if you have taxable income above about $22,000, then $1 of SS is withheld per $2 of earnings above the $22,000. Not to worry, when you reach your full retirement age, you get the withheld money back. But those withheld dollars can’t be invested from age 62-67. Next, you can’t just “toss your SS check into an index fund and make 6% after inflation.” First, those capital gains might be taxed at 0, 15, or even 20%. More importantly, those are not guaranteed. Social security goes up 8% per year of delayed filing, PLUS inflation. And those increases, unlike the aforementioned index funds, are not subject to taxation along the way. So filing early and index funding vs delayed filing is comparing a speculative taxable strategy with a guaranteed tax deferred strategy.

It’s not taxable income that counts towards the $22,000, it is earned income. The two can be quite different (think dividends, interest, capital gains vs. salary).

You can certainly include NPV of SS in your Net Worth Statement. It is an Asset (it has monetary value). An asset doesn’t need to be immediately convertible to cash in order to count as an asset – there are simple examples such as a house (that takes time and has costs associated in turning the asset into ‘money’) and more complicated ones like REITs and annuities. They are all Assets as they have monetary value.

What is probably more logical to do is including SS as a Retirement Asset – or those assets you plan to live off of in retirement. This is often a different list of assets than what is in your Net Worth Statement – and is used for a different purpose (creating a stream of cash to live off of in retirement).

I’ve always questioned the “better to wait to withdraw for maximum benefits” position. That may be true for non-mustachians who need every dollar of SS to live on and are willing to work longer to maximize their annual income. But SS’s early and delayed adjustments are actuarially derived to ensure the total cost to the system is the same. Theoretically, you would receive the same amount over your lifetime. Claiming earlier is a hedge against dying young. Unless you have a crystal ball and are assured of living longer than average, it’s better to claim early and invest. I looked into this a few years ago, and came across the paper: https://crr.bc.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/IB_19-18.pdf

It’s a great summary of the history of delayed and early options (early claiming was originally designed to allow the younger spouse to not be penalized for retiring with the older spouse). It also analyzes whether the assumptions for the original actuarial adjustments apply today. Summary: adjustments for taking early (65) are probably right. It’s a wash to take anytime after 65. However, higher earners live longer and delay more. If delayed adjustments were based on those who actually use it, the increase should be less. Based on increased life expectancies, wealthier individuals should wait.

I want to call out a couple considerations around the longevity of Social Security and Medicare for those in the USA.

First, there is a provision within the Social Security legislation that stipulates should Social Security funding be deficient to pay out all intended benefits, it will still pay out based on its annual tax intake. While the Social Security funding is quickly dwindling, the expectation is that the annual tax intake will continue to represent ~80% of intended benefits. Thus, even if you don’t expect Congress to actively fix Social Security funding, unless you expect Congress to actively kill Social Security then you should expect some payout.

That said, it is important to note that Medicare has no such deficiency stipulation in its legislation, so if Medicare funding becomes deficient then without an active effort from Congress it will just be gone. I know that early retirees typically plan for medical coverage between retirement and becoming Medicare eligible, but I’ve seen many assume Medicare will be there, which it may not. On one hand, ACA coverage creates a cost-capped option at age 65+, but that assumes that ACA coverage is still around. I know MMM has also suggested options such as self-funding or community plans, but I’ll warn that those are generally more viable for those early retirement years and become generally less viable for many as you get into your golden years. This is where HSAs can be really helpful, and since they can double up as 401k-like funds for non-medical expenses after 65, I really do recommend taking advantage of them as best as you can. Everyone’s costs and longevity will vary, and potentially significantly so if you require long-term care, but there is a general rule of thumb of trying to have ~$200k/person at age 65 bucketed for retirement medical expenses (premiums and out-of-pocket costs), where the expectation is that bucket should continue to grow despite withdrawals in the early years and then transition to mostly drawing down as you get further up in the years.

Please consider using a discount rate that meets the criteria of the “next best option of similar risk.” That is standard practice for discount rates. In this case, TIPS would be a natural choice. Their inflation-adjusted discount rate would be ~2%.

After all – if we’re going to neglect risk, why not use Berkshire Hathaway’s historical return of 20% per year? Or Bitcoin’s of 230% per year?

Using the proper 2% instead of 6% would lead us to the opposite conclusion as this article. That is, claiming at 62 is the WORST choice if you’ll live until 90.

I realize this might torpedo the entire article. But it’ll also lead the audience to reach better retirement conclusions.

I’m excited to see this topic! Most people I ask (including financial advisors and moneywise folks) insist that it’s almost always better to defer drawing Social Security until normal retirement age (67) or even later (70). However, most people don’t understand the time value of money! I retired four years ago at age 57 and I’m very much looking forward to drawing Social Security next year at age 62. Why? Because it’s a much, much better deal. Here’ s how it works. Using the data provided to me by the Social Security Administration, my current estimated monthly benefit amounts will be $2,513 if starting at age 62, or $3,569 if starting at age 67, and $4,425 if starting at age 70. It appears obvious that it would be best to wait for the higher amount. But it is not. Here’s why. In a zero-interest rate world, I can run a simple break-even analysis and determine that it would take me until age 78½ to come out ahead by waiting until 67 to start. It would take me until age 80½ to break even if I waited until 70 to start. With a current life expectancy for me to live until age 76½, I’m still better off to start at age 62, but only slightly. But then again, we don’t live in a zero-interest rate world! In a 4% interest rate world, these figures change dramatically. It now takes me until age 85½ to break even when starting at age 67, and until age 87 when starting at age 70. In an 8% interest rate world (The S&P 500 has averaged 10.5% annually since 1957), my break-even points are both now out beyond 100 years old. It’s really a no-brainer!

If the USD collapses, basically all of our retirement planning goes out the window. I suppose if you felt *really sure* that it was coming, you could try to invest your money primarily in foreign markets… but then, all of those markets are also strongly tied to the USD, so you’re still in a bad spot *and* you’ll have been missing out on the high growth of US Index Fund in the interim (so even if it “falls less”, it wouldn’t have grown as high before falling…). I guess you could stockpile physical gold, but that has it’s own problems and risks.

My personal take on this (and many other “catastrophic global collapse” events) is A) Basically every member of society has a vested interest in not allowing it to happen, so it’s probably not very likely, and B) if you really think it is going to happen, where you invest your money probably won’t matter, and instead you should probably invest your time and money in planning how to survive it.

There’s a whole prepper culture around this, but if you’re truly worried about it, you’d want to have some remote land with a fresh water source, with shelter, and tools, and crops, and livestock, basically you’ll want to be as self-sufficient as possible. Of course, all of that stuff does you no good if you don’t know how to use it, and if society collapses and you realize you’re missing an important tool, you can’t just order it off Amazon any more. Ultimately the conclusion I reached is essentially, “If you really want to be set up to survive the collapse of society, you need to start living like society has collapsed already.” I decided I didn’t really want to live that way, so I’ve stopped worrying about it all that much.

Hey Pete, Regarding your comment on you won’t care about the taxes on your RMDs when you’re 75 because you’ll have plenty of income. I take issue with that as a 75 year old with a six figure retirement income living a comfy life in expensive Boulder County like you. I don’t want to pay taxes to a federal government that is spending in areas that are not my values. But that’s not my main point. Only a couple people have commented on SS taxability (e.g., Jiri, Dave) aside from taxes on RMDs. Not everyone realizes that up to 85% of your SS income is taxable depending on what other kinds of annual retirement income you have. The IRS uses a formula where tax-deferred pensions, royalties, 401K distributions, and any earned income can trigger the taxability of your SS payment. The way to potentially avoid this with the present laws is to pay taxes on any future funds when you’re working, i.e., Roth contributions, Roth conversions, and backdoor Roths if you’re over the Roth eligibility limits. This works best for 1099 people, but W-2 people also can benefit from it to a lesser extent. I’m a believer it’s not how much you make, but how much you keep from the government.

However, if you are a high earner in your working years, it makes sense to max the traditional retirements accounts to avoid a (currently) 24% or 32% tax rate (which was actually quite a bit higher in the past), not worry as much about Roth, and then pay the tax on Social Security. Odds are that the tax on your Social Security will fall in the 12% bracket, or maybe 22% if you are making particularly substantial withdrawals from traditional retirement accounts.

#8430. 13 Night Jobs That Fit Around Your Days – Ask Whether Nights Pay More

For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Night and evening work lets you earn extra money without giving up your days, from overnight stocking, security, and caregiving shifts to delivery and tutoring gigs you schedule yourself. Before you take an employer’s night shift, ask whether it pays a shift differential, a premium for night hours, since the federal minimum wage and overtime law doesn’t require one.

These hours suit night owls, students with daytime classes, parents who trade shifts with a partner, and anyone adding paid hours after a day job.

The Department of Labor says extra pay for night work is a matter for you and the employer to agree on, or for a union that represents you. The federal government, for one, adds 10% to the basic pay of employees on its General Schedule pay scale for regularly scheduled work between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m., the Office of Personnel Management says.

The pay below is each job’s median hourly wage for May 2025 from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, tips included. Those medians leave out shift differentials, so a night premium would come on top. If a store pays its overnight stockers $2 an hour more than its day crew, 30 hours of night work a week bring in $60 more than the same hours by day.

These pay by the trip, the order, or the tutoring hour, and you choose when to log on. The driving numbers come from Gridwise, an app drivers use to track their earnings, for the third quarter of 2026, and they’re gross pay, before your gas, car wear, and taxes. Work out your hourly pay after costs before you count on one.

If the night job will be your second one, adjust the tax withheld from your paychecks and check your main employer’s rules on taking a second job before the first shift.

A night premium can cover only part of a shift, the way the federal one counts only hours between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. Before you accept an employer’s night shift, ask what it pays per hour at night and which hours earn that rate.

#8428. Splurge on Foundation, Save on Mascara – Pay More for Makeup That Shows and Lasts

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Pay high-end prices only for makeup you wear on your whole face every day, which mostly means foundation, and test it with a free sample before you buy. Start with drugstore mascara, eyeliner, and lip color, since manufacturers usually recommend replacing mascara every few months, whatever you paid for it.

A department-store brand and a drugstore brand can belong to the same company. L’Oréal, which owns both Lancôme and Maybelline New York, spent 32.2% of its 2025 sales on advertising and promotion, about 10 times what went to research and innovation.

So a higher price doesn’t prove a better formula. Pay more only where the difference shows every day and you’ll use the product long enough to get your money’s worth.

Foundation qualifies. It covers your whole face every day, so a shade that’s slightly off is easy to spot, and it usually stays usable longer than eye makeup. The FDA notes that eye-area products tend to go bad faster than other cosmetics, and that manufacturers usually recommend throwing mascara out two to four months after purchase.

That makes mascara the easiest place to save, because you pay any premium again with every new tube. At one tube every three months, a $30 department-store mascara costs $120 a year, against $48 for a $12 drugstore tube. The gap is $72 a year on one product.

Try drugstore eyeliner and lip color first too, and buy them where one that disappoints can go back. Ulta Beauty, which stocks drugstore brands, refunds most new or gently used products returned within 30 days of purchase, so keep the receipt.

For foundation, test before you pay. Sephora stores offer a free shade match with a skin-tone scanner, and you can ask a Beauty Advisor for a free sample of any brand in any shade. Look up dupes too, cheaper products that closely match a pricier one, and read reviews that compare the two side by side.

Wear the sample through a full day and check it in daylight, then buy the bottle only if it still matches.

#8427. Piolets d'Or Insider: How the Jury Works, Style Debates, and Future Plans

The recent 2026 edition of the Piolets d’Or awards, held last week in a remote corner of the French Alps, felt like an organization trying to adapt to fast-changing times and attract larger audiences while keeping its prestige and spirit intact.

ExplorersWeb was there to meet old acquaintances and to put a face to some of the names we wrote about in the last 12 months. We also wanted to participate in the collective exercise of reflection about the future.

Views of Les Ecrins Massif from Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Piolet d’Or recipients enjoyed a relaxed atmosphere at the tiny village of Saint-Christophe-en-Oisans and a ceremony at Burg d’Oisans, a 30-minute drive down the valley. Yet, the most interesting event took place the following day, as an elite group of climbers sat around a table in a small hall with large glass windows facing autumn-colored forests and the ragged peaks of the Ecrins Massif, covered in the first snow dust of the season.

Representing the awardees were Nicolas Jean (awarded for climbing Jannu East with Benjamin Vedrines); the complete teams from Ultar Shar, Aikache Chokk, and Jerupaja Grande; a hyper-energetic, widely smiling Peter Habeler, 84, who received a lifetime achievement Piolet d’Or; Simon Welfringer, who gave a talk; organizers Christian Trommsdorf and David Chambre; geographer and chronicler Rodolphe Popier, and two members of the jury: Jordi Corminas of Spain and Paul Ramsden of the UK. At a press conference, these experts debated some of the hot issues in today’s mountaineering.

Simon Welfringer of France speaks at the post-Piolets d’Or experts’ panel. Photo: Angela Benavides

Trommsdorf noted that the jury had an easy time selecting the awarded climbs this year. He explained how these expert jurists choose the best alpine-style activities of the year.

The members work remotely, choosing from a Big List of outstanding activities. This list is previously compiled by Lindsay Griffin, long-time editor of the American Alpine Journal, and the UK’s Alpine Club. Jurors study the climbs and narrow it down to a short list of candidates, which is not made public. The awards go to those activities chosen by the majority of jury members. In this case, decisions were finalized on the first vote, with no need for a tie-break.

Left to right, Rodolphe Popier, Jordi Corominas, Paul Ramsden (speaking), and David Chambre. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

That led to the first topic of debate: It was noted that some climbing teams happily announce themselves as “Piolet d’Or nominates” on social media when their climbs appear on the Big List — although organizers make it clear that not all activities on that list are suitable for a Piolet d’Or. Yet, no one supported the idea of making the short lists public. The general agreement was to keep the small “best of the year” finalists available only to the jury.

The second topic for debate was the presence of a relatively new piece of technology now ubiquitous on expeditions: drones. These have become essential on rescues, but climbing teams also use them to scout the route ahead. In the near future, drones could also carry supplies, emergency kits, or extra equipment. Commercial outfitters are already using them in this way.

Benjamin Vedrines and Nicolas Jean of France used drones to check the state of their planned route on Jannu. However, they explained that the drone was useless in relaying information about a section that they couldn’t see from Base Camp. It had a different angle of view, and the drone lost connection when it tried to approach that area.

Drones piloted by their base camp film crew also hovered overhead as they traversed the long summit ridge. Finally, before the summit push, they used drones to clearly identify the highest point, to make sure they reached the true summit.

The Ultar Sar team also had a drone, they noted. All the awarded climbers agreed that drones are okay as long as the climbers are completely transparent about what they used them for. Jordi Corominas said the drones are a technological innovation that has come to stay, no different than InReach devices, satphones, or even ice axes and crampons.

Jordi Corominas, left, discusses past climbs with Benjamin Vedrines. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

Interestingly, one jurist stood against the tide: Paul Ramsden is an advocate for the pure alpine-style criteria of the UK climbing school, and with five Piolets d’Or, he is the overall record holder of these prestigious awards. In his opinion, drones spoil the adventure and uncertainty inherent in pure alpine style. Ramsden himself uses neither drones, trackers, nor even satphones.

Finally, Trommsdor suggested possibly expanding the awards to create a special Piolet d’Or for the best rock climb and perhaps even the best ski descent. The idea expand on the new performance category introduced this year in the big list as a test. The category featured, among others, the two Everest ski descents in 2025. Both were heavily supported, and Jim Morrison‘s descent of the Hornbein Couloir was oxygen-assisted.

In the end, one of the performance ski descents received the female award: Typhaine Duperier‘s alpine-style climb+ski descent of Nanga Parbat’s Schell route, with Boris Langenstein.

It is unclear whether the new additions will become official in the near future, but some attendees expressed concern about the context in which these take place. Would they award ski expeditions for their boldness or technical excellence without bearing in mind how the skiers reached the start of their descent (supported climbs, fixed routes, even helicopters)?

As for rock climbs: where to set the difference between a rock climb and an alpine climb on high, but dry, faces? The debate was left open. We will find out what, if anything, changes in the next edition of the Piolets d’Or.

Buried houses at the now abandoned village of La Berarde. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

The physical award is no longer an actual piolet (ice axe). In the last few years, it has been a hand-crafted trophy that changes with the venue. This time, it was a plaque with a reproduction of Ecrins National Park’s most distinctive peak, La Meige. It rested on a piece of rock from the remains of La Berarde, a nearby village destroyed in a flood two years ago.

At the Piolets d’Or ceremony in Burg d’Oisans. Photo: Angela Benavides

Next year, the Piolets d’Or will be staged in the same location, perhaps in late summer. The event will commemorate the 150th anniversary of the first ascent of La Meige. The long-term plan is to turn the Piolet d’Or ceremony into a bigger, international mountain festival.

Angela Benavides graduated university in journalism and specializes in high-altitude mountaineering and expedition news. She has been writing about climbing and mountaineering, adventure and outdoor sports for 20+ years.

Prior to that, Angela Benavides spent time at/worked at a number of local and international media. She is also experienced in outdoor-sport consultancy for sponsoring corporations, press manager and communication executive, and a published author.

ExplorersWeb is part of AllGear Digital's portfolio of media brands.

#8426. Financing Your First Rental? Expect 15% to 25% Down and a Higher Rate

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Finance a rental property with a conventional investment mortgage when your income qualifies, or a DSCR loan, which looks at the rent instead, when it doesn’t. Either way, plan on 15% to 25% down, a rate at least half a percentage point above a home loan’s, and several months of payments in savings. Get preapproved before you make offers.

Lenders charge more on a home you won’t live in because the loan is riskier for them.

If your income qualifies, start with a conventional investment mortgage. Under Freddie Mac rules, it takes 25% down on a building with two to four units and as little as 15% on a single-family rental. Below 20% down, you’ll also pay for mortgage insurance. A duplex you’ll live in counts as your home instead and can take 5% down.

A DSCR loan, short for debt service coverage ratio, qualifies you on how well the property’s rent covers its payment instead of on your income. It usually costs more than a conventional loan, so it’s the fallback when your income won’t qualify, and DSCR lenders often want a credit score of at least 680 and 20% to 25% down. Some banks also make portfolio loans, which they keep rather than sell, so they set their own terms.

On a conventional loan, Fannie Mae’s reserve rule asks for six months of the rental’s full payment, taxes and insurance included, in savings, investments, or vested retirement money. Its rental income rule counts 75% of the expected rent, and if you’ve managed rentals for less than a year, that rent can only cover the property’s own payment, never count as income.

Borrowing the down payment against your own house, with a home equity line of credit, puts the house at risk unless your paycheck can repay the line. Telling a lender you’ll live in a home you plan to rent is what the Federal Housing Finance Agency calls occupancy fraud.

Say you buy a $250,000 rental with 25% down and a 30-year fixed loan at 7.75%, against 7% on a home loan. You’d bring $62,500 plus closing costs and six months of payments in reserve, and pay about $1,343 a month in principal and interest, $96 more than the same loan’s $1,247 at 7%.

Get preapproved by two or three lenders, one of them a local bank or credit union, for the loan you’ll use before you make an offer.

To find lenders for those preapprovals, compare the best mortgage lenders.

#8425. Seller Financing Makes You the Lender – Vet the Buyer Like a Bank Would

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Offer seller financing on your house only if it’s paid off or your mortgage lender agrees in writing. You become the buyer’s lender, so protect yourself the way a bank would, with a credit and income check, at least 10% down, a real estate attorney to draft the note, and a loan servicing company to collect it.

Lending to the buyer opens your house to people a bank won’t approve, which can sell it faster or for more, and pays you interest. It also leaves you with the lender’s risk that the payments stop.

The buyer signs a promissory note, an IOU setting the rate, the term, and any balloon, the lump sum due at the end. A mortgage or deed of trust recorded in your favor gives you the right to foreclose if they default.

Federal rules for loan originators, the professionals who arrange mortgages, don’t apply to a homeowner who finances only one sale in any 12-month period. A balloon doesn’t change that, as long as the payments never let the balance grow and the rate is fixed, or adjusts only after five years, on the rules’ terms. If you still owe on the house, check your mortgage for a due-on-sale clause, which lets the lender demand the full balance if you sell without first getting its written consent.

Before you close, put these protections in place.

Say you sell a paid-off $250,000 house with $25,000 down and finance the other $225,000 at 7%, with payments set as if the loan ran 30 years and the balance due after five. You’d collect about $1,497 a month, then about $212,000 when the buyer refinances to pay the balloon.

Until then, most of your sale price stays tied up in the loan. The interest is taxable income, and any taxable profit on the sale can be reported as the payments arrive. Offer financing only with money you won’t need until the note is paid off.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

#8424. Drinking Costs More Than the Bar Tab – Total It, Then Try a Dry Month

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

What you spend on drinking comes in small charges that are easy to miss: bar tabs, bottles for home, tips, delivery fees, and rides home. Add up a month of them, then try a month without alcohol, set a weekly spending limit after it, and move the difference into savings.

The average household spent $630 on alcohol in 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reports, and that figure includes households that don’t drink at all.

Say a couple spends $90 a week on drinks out and $30 on bottles for home. That’s $480 every four weeks and $6,240 a year, nearly 10 times the $630 average, before counting any rides home.

To find your own number, go through last month’s card and bank statements. Add up every bar tab with its tip, every bottle bought for home, every alcohol delivery and its fees, and every ride home from a night out, plus any cash you spent at bars. Multiply that total by 12 to see what drinking costs you in a year.

Then go a month without drinking. Use Dry January or any month with no wedding, vacation, or big birthday on the calendar. Each week, move what you would have spent, about a quarter of last month’s total, into a high-yield savings account. The couple above would have $480 put away after four weeks. If going without is harder than you expected, call SAMHSA’s National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357. The federal line is free, confidential, and open 24/7, and it refers callers to local treatment, support groups, and community organizations.

Once the month is over, a few habits keep the cost down without cutting the ride home. Swap some bar nights for a potluck at home or other cheap things to do with friends, alternate each drink with a glass of water, and go out at happy hour, when drinks cost less.

Set a weekly limit on what you spend on drinks, and keep moving the difference between that limit and your old weekly spending into savings.

To choose where those weekly savings go, compare the best high-yield savings accounts.

#8423. Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend.

So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

In private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better. Here are three simple steps to follow:

1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

2) Drive an old car.  Driving a new car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

Once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

My parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

At the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 31-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

Then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

And you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

Today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such conspicuous spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? We think to ourselves. But we’re missing something important.

Her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

This resonated with me as a minority who came to America for high school and faced various racist incidents. Racism is one of the deepest forms of disrespect because you're insulted just for being who you are. Respect, especially for elders, is a big part of Asian culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

When you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

At 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

Then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

Today, insults from random folks feel more like pinches instead of body blows. The passive income is doing its job as a shield.

As a dad now, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no big deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

In that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the big deal?

Yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

Reaching FIRE doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect.

Maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

Whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else. Know that there is an incredible joy of being a nobody so long as you have your finances in order.

For many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

That’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

Readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

Stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

I’m not quite sure that I follow some of the logic here, and wonder whether a couple of concepts are getting confounded.

“Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.”

Well, if I feel better wearing clothes which are not a baseball hat and sneakers, then this isn’t great advice. These are your tastes, and your solution to the problem, but you can’t know that they will work for others. In many cultural contexts, even Western ones, your clothing suggestions are inappropriate: One is unlikely to be well-received in a courtroom or at a funeral dressed like that. Indeed, wearing your suggestions in some contexts is quite clearly going to draw attention to you, and make you stand out, yet I believe that’s what you’re trying to avoid.

I lunched with a recently-fired, job-seeking friend last week, who expressed surprised that I would come to our mid-week lunch in a tavern wearing a “suit”, despite my having retired last month. Leaving aside the detail that I wasn’t wearing a suit at all, but a sports jacket, it seemed not to have occurred to him that I’m now free to wear what I like, which is a sports jacket, rather than being subtly pressured as a tech-company employee to wear ghastly slim-fit chinos and a plain polo shirt.

I suppose I don’t really know what you mean by “fancy clothes”, but one should probably seek to dress as one sees oneself. Clothing is a communication channel, after all.

“Drive an old car. Driving a new car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.”

This advice seems to confound two distinct things. You’re against both new cars and luxury brands, which are two utterly different things. What about a new car from a budget brand? What about buying an old car from a luxury brand? What about choosing a car which means your needs and reflects your self-image?

What point exactly are you trying to make? If one gets a lot of pleasure from owning and driving a sports car, then why should one follow your advice?

Good points – in terms of stealth wealth, the “regular” clothes and standard used car would probably be the defaults.

Agreed – in certain social settings a suit or jacket is respectful and considered appropriate. But in many places, wearing a nice suit while stepping out of a luxury car wouldn’t be considered stealth wealth, whatever the personal motivations.

But, I agree – people should in general wear what they enjoy etc. And higher quality items generally are more enjoyable to use, so it can be a dilemma to practice stealth wealth while enjoying a custom made Italian suit!
